---
title: "Exploring a database"
---

Once you have [downloaded the demo data](demo-data.html), take a few minutes to
get familiar with the results. This guide uses the HepG2 DIA database to inspect
the experiment, find available measurements, and retrieve a small table in R.
Run the examples in order in the same R session. The tables below are generated
from the demo database when this article is built.

## 1. Open the database

Load ProteoVaultR and dplyr, then open the file you downloaded. Here we use the
`demo-data` directory from the download guide; adjust the path if you saved the
file elsewhere. For documentation builds, `PROTEOVAULTR_DEMO_DIR` can point to
the directory containing the cached databases.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(ProteoVaultR)
library(dplyr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r open-vault}
data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROTEOVAULTR_DEMO_DIR", unset = "demo-data")
vault <- open_vault(
    path = file.path(data_dir, "hepg2_ifna-dia.proteovault.duckdb")
)
vault
```

`vault` is your connection to the database. Printing it gives a short description
of the dataset, schema version, available layers, and file location. Opening it
does not load all the measurements into R, and the database remains read-only.

::: {.alert .alert-warning role="note"}
**Keep the connection open:** The queries below use `vault` to read the database.
Close it after you have collected the results you need.
:::

## 2. Inspect the experiment

Use `vault_info()` to see how the database was assembled:

```{r inspect-vault}
info <- vault_info(vault)
info$analysis %>%
    select(dataset_id, pipeline, pipeline_version) %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Dataset", "Pipeline", "Version")
    )
```

The imported layers tell you which additional results are available:

```{r inspect-layers}
info$layers
```


`info$analysis` records the dataset and pipeline version. Layers describe the
kinds of results imported into the database. Additional layers may contain QC
metrics, protein sequences, or annotations; not every database includes them all.

### 2.1. Look at samples and acquisition runs

Read the sample names stored in the database:

```{r inspect-samples}
samples <- tbl_vault(vault, "samples") %>%
    select(sample_id, sample_name) %>%
    arrange(sample_name) %>%
    collect()

samples %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Sample ID", "Sample name")
    )
```

Use these names when you add experimental metadata later. For the HepG2 DIA
example, each sample corresponds to an unfractionated acquisition. A fractionated
experiment can have several runs per sample, so it is useful to inspect both:

```{r inspect-runs}
runs <- tbl_vault(vault, "runs") %>%
    select(run_id, sample_id, run_name, file_name) %>%
    collect()

runs %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Run ID", "Sample ID", "Run name", "File name")
    )
```

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**TMT samples and runs:** One acquisition measures a plex containing several
reporter channels. Quantitative sample names use `<plex_id>|<reporter_label>`,
so a run and a quantitative sample represent different parts of the experiment.
:::

### 2.2. See the available tables

```{r inspect-tables}
list_vault_tables(vault)
```

This lists the tables and views present in the open database. `tbl_vault()` lets
you inspect one by name. For common tasks, the dedicated query functions below
provide a more convenient starting point.

## 3. Find the measurements you need

ProteoVault keeps track of both the **source file** and the **measurement method**.
A source identifies an imported result file; a method identifies the quantity it
provides, such as a matrix value or a particular report quantity. Inspect them
before deciding which measurements to use.

```{r inspect-methods}
measurements <- tbl_vault(vault, "source_quant_methods") %>%
    inner_join(tbl_vault(vault, "quant_methods"), by = "method_id") %>%
    inner_join(tbl_vault(vault, "source_files"), by = "source_id") %>%
    select(level, method = name, source_id, relative_path) %>%
    arrange(level, method, relative_path) %>%
    collect()

measurements %>%
    mutate(relative_path = basename(relative_path)) %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Level", "Method", "Source ID", "Source file")
    )
```

The `level` column distinguishes protein-group, peptide, and precursor quantities.
The available methods depend on the workflow and imported files. This inventory
helps you choose a method without guessing from a filename.

| What you want to explore | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Protein-group quantities | `tbl_protein_quant()` |
| Native peptide quantities from DDA ProteinQuantifier | `tbl_peptide_quant()` |
| Precursor quantities | `tbl_precursor_quant()` |
| Validated peptide-spectrum matches | `tbl_psms()` |
| Protein groups and their members | `tbl_protein_groups()` and `tbl_group_members()` |

A precursor is a modified peptide with a particular charge. DIA peptide-level
summaries are derived from precursor quantities when preparing an assay; they are
not the native DDA peptide measurements returned by `tbl_peptide_quant()`.

## 4. Retrieve a small table

For the HepG2 DIA example, start with protein-group quantities from the imported
matrix. Select the matching source explicitly:

```{r select-quantities}
method <- "matrix"
source_id <- resolve_quant_source(
    vault,
    level = "protein_group",
    method = method
)

protein_quant <- tbl_protein_quant(
    vault,
    source_id = source_id,
    method = method
)

source_id
```

::: {.alert .alert-warning role="note"}
**Choose the matching source:** If several sources provide the requested method,
select a `source_id` from the measurement inventory. For another dataset or
quantity, use the method and source recorded in that database.
:::

Now select positive quantities from the first sample and retrieve just ten rows:

```{r preview-quantities}
first_sample <- samples$sample_name[[1L]]

preview <- protein_quant %>%
    filter(sample_name == first_sample, quantity > 0) %>%
    select(sample_name, source_group_id, quantity) %>%
    arrange(source_group_id) %>%
    head(10) %>%
    collect()

preview %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Sample", "Protein group", "Quantity"),
        digits = 2
    )
```

Here, `source_group_id` is the original protein-group label and `quantity` is the
stored measurement. These are group-level quantities; a group can contain more
than one protein.

Until `collect()`, this is a **lazy query**: filtering and selection take place in
DuckDB. `collect()` brings the selected rows into an R table.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Tip:** Filter and limit rows before calling `collect()`. Here, `head(10)` keeps
the preview small even when the database contains many results.
:::

## 5. Close the connection

```{r close-vault}
close_vault(vault)
vault
```

The collected `samples`, `runs`, `measurements`, and `preview` tables remain
available in R. The lazy `protein_quant` query needs an open connection; reopen
the database and recreate the query if you want to continue using it.

You now know how to find and retrieve results. Continue with [Preparing data](preparing-data.html) to connect those
measurements with your sample metadata and prepare a quantitative matrix for
analysis. For more about any function used here, see the
[function reference](../reference/index.html).
